questions.q: A 28-year-old man presents with a painless, indurated ulcer on the glans penis for 3 weeks. Inguinal lymph nodes are enlarged and non-tender. Dark-field microscopy of the serous exudate shows corkscrew-shaped organisms with characteristic motility. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.exp: Primary syphilis presents as a painless indurated ulcer (chancre) with non-tender regional lymphadenopathy. Dark-field microscopy reveals Treponema pallidum with characteristic cork-screw motility and end-on rotation.

questions.q: A 35-year-old farmer presents with a 6-month history of a slowly enlarging plaque on the dorsum of the foot with multiple sinuses discharging white granules. KOH examination of the granules reveals broad, branching, septate hyphae. The most appropriate treatment is:
questions.exp: White grain mycetoma is caused by eumycetes (true fungi), commonly Pseudallescheria boydii. Eumycetoma is treated with itraconazole + terbinafine combination. Bacterial actinomycetoma (which produces white granules with Nocardia brasiliensis) uses co-trimoxazole + amikacin.

questions.q: A 22-year-old woman presents with a 2-week history of tense bullae on normal and erythematous skin, predominantly on the inner thighs, groins, and abdomen. Nikolsky sign is negative. Direct immunofluorescence shows linear IgG and C3 deposition at the dermoepidermal junction. The most likely diagnosis is:
questions.exp: Bullous pemphigoid presents with tense bullae on erythematous skin, negative Nikolsky sign, and linear IgG + C3 at BMZ on DIF. The target antigens are BP180 (type XVII collagen) and BP230. It is the most common autoimmune bullous disorder in adults.

questions.q: A 40-year-old woman with long-standing systemic lupus erythematosus develops a blistering eruption on sun-exposed areas. Biopsy shows subepidermal blister. DIF reveals linear IgG, IgA, and C3 at the BMZ, and salt-split skin shows deposits on the dermal side. The diagnosis is:
questions.exp: Epidermolysis bullosa acquisita (EBA) is caused by autoantibodies against type VII collagen at the anchoring fibrils. On salt-split skin (1M NaCl), antibodies deposit on the dermal floor (vs. epidermal roof in BP). Bullous SLE also targets type VII collagen but responds dramatically to dapsone.

questions.q: A 55-year-old man presents with a 2-cm pearly nodule on the nose with rolled borders, central ulceration, and surface telangiectasia. He has a 30-year history of outdoor sun exposure. Biopsy reveals islands of basaloid cells with peripheral palisading and retraction artifact. The best initial treatment is:
opts: Wide local excision with 2 cm margins
questions.exp: Nodular basal cell carcinoma on the nose (high-risk H-zone) is best treated with Mohs micrographic surgery, which provides >99% cure rates by examining 100% of surgical margins in frozen sections while sparing maximal normal tissue. Standard excision with 4 mm margins is an alternative for low-risk BCCs.

questions.q: A 30-year-old patient with leprosy on MDT for 8 months develops sudden onset of painful, erythematous, tender nodules over both arms and legs with fever and joint pains. ESR is elevated. This reaction is best managed with:
questions.exp: This is Type 2 lepra reaction (Erythema Nodosum Leprosum - ENL), an immune complex (Type III hypersensitivity) mediated reaction seen in BL/LL leprosy. Thalidomide is the drug of choice for recurrent/severe ENL in non-childbearing individuals; prednisolone is also used. MDT must never be stopped and should be continued throughout.

questions.q: A 25-year-old man presents with a well-defined hypopigmented patch on the left cheek with diminished sensation to touch and temperature. A thickened greater auricular nerve is palpable. Slit-skin smear is negative. The Ridley-Jopling classification of this patient is:
questions.exp: Tuberculoid leprosy (TT) presents with a single, well-defined hypopigmented patch with complete loss of sensation, prominent nerve thickening, and negative smear. The patch has sharp, raised inner borders. TT has the highest cell-mediated immunity and lowest bacillary load on the leprosy spectrum.

questions.q: A 19-year-old female presents with sharply demarcated erythematous plaques with silvery-white scales on the knees and elbows since age 15. Removal of scales reveals pinpoint bleeding spots. Nail examination shows pitting, onycholysis, and oil drop sign. The Auspitz sign is positive. The underlying mechanism involves:
questions.exp: Psoriasis is driven by Th1 and Th17 cells, with key cytokines TNF-alpha, IL-17, and IL-23 leading to keratinocyte hyperproliferation. Epidermal transit time is reduced from 28 days to 3-4 days. Auspitz sign reflects dilated capillaries in dermal papillae exposed after scale removal (Munro microabscesses).

questions.q: A 45-year-old woman on methotrexate for psoriasis develops nausea, oral ulcers, and macrocytic anemia. The drug responsible for this toxicity acts by:
questions.exp: Methotrexate inhibits dihydrofolate reductase (DHFR), depleting tetrahydrofolate needed for thymidylate synthesis and purine synthesis, causing toxicity in rapidly dividing cells (gut epithelium, bone marrow). Folic acid 5 mg/week (not on MTX day) reduces mucosal and hematological toxicity. Regular LFTs and CBC monitoring are essential.

questions.q: A 32-year-old man presents with pruritic, coin-shaped, erythematous plaques on both legs with crusting and weeping. The plaques are well-defined with satellite vesicles at the margins. He has no personal or family history of atopy. The most likely diagnosis is:
questions.exp: Nummular eczema (discoid eczema) presents as coin-shaped, pruritic, weeping plaques predominantly on the legs of middle-aged men. Unlike atopic dermatitis, there is no atopic association. Secondary bacterial infection with S. aureus is common. Treatment includes potent topical corticosteroids and emollients.

questions.q: A 5-year-old child presents with honey-colored crusted lesions around the nostrils and mouth for 5 days. Culture grows coagulase-positive, gram-positive cocci. The first-line topical treatment is:
questions.exp: Non-bullous impetigo is caused by S. aureus (and sometimes S. pyogenes). Mupirocin 2% ointment is the first-line topical antibiotic, acting by inhibiting bacterial isoleucyl-tRNA synthetase. For widespread lesions, oral flucloxacillin or cefalexin is used. Fusidic acid is an alternative but has higher resistance rates.

questions.q: A 60-year-old diabetic woman presents with unilateral painful vesicles along the T5 dermatome on the right side for 3 days. What is the drug of choice and the window period for maximum antiviral efficacy?
opts: Acyclovir 800 mg 5 times/day; within 72 hours of rash onset
questions.exp: Herpes zoster is treated with oral acyclovir 800 mg 5 times daily for 7 days, valacyclovir 1 g thrice daily, or famciclovir 500 mg thrice daily. Treatment is most effective within 72 hours of rash onset. In immunocompromised patients, IV acyclovir 10 mg/kg 8-hourly is used. Antivirals reduce PHN risk.

questions.q: A 25-year-old HIV-positive man presents with multiple cauliflower-like warty growths around the anus and perianal region. HPV typing reveals HPV types 6 and 11. The most appropriate patient-applied treatment is:
questions.exp: Condylomata acuminata caused by HPV 6 and 11 (low-risk types) can be treated with patient-applied imiquimod 5% (TLR-7 agonist, immune modifier) 3 times weekly for up to 16 weeks, or podophyllotoxin 0.5%. Physician-applied options include cryotherapy and TCA. Imiquimod has lower recurrence rates than podophyllin.

questions.q: A 38-year-old woman develops a butterfly-shaped erythema across both cheeks sparing the nasolabial folds. She has photosensitivity, oral ulcers, and ANA titer 1:640 with anti-dsDNA positivity. The most specific antibody for this condition is:
questions.exp: Anti-Sm (anti-Smith) antibody is the most specific antibody for SLE (specificity ~99%), though sensitivity is only 25-30%. Anti-dsDNA is both specific (95%) and correlates with disease activity/nephritis. Anti-Ro/SSA is associated with neonatal lupus and subacute cutaneous lupus. Anti-histone indicates drug-induced lupus.

questions.q: A 50-year-old woman presents with Raynaud's phenomenon, skin tightening proximal to the MCPJs, dysphagia, and pulmonary fibrosis on HRCT. ANA shows a nucleolar pattern, and anti-Scl-70 is positive. The diagnosis is:
questions.exp: Diffuse cutaneous systemic sclerosis (dcSSc) involves skin proximal to MCPJs including the trunk, with early visceral involvement (pulmonary fibrosis, renal crisis) and anti-Scl-70 (anti-topoisomerase I). Limited SSc (CREST syndrome) has skin restricted to face and distal limbs, anti-centromere antibody, and pulmonary arterial hypertension as the main complication.

questions.q: A 4-year-old child presents with perioral and perianal dermatitis, alopecia, and diarrhea after weaning from breast milk. Serum zinc is 28 mcg/dL (normal 70-110). The condition results from deficiency of which transporter?
questions.exp: Acrodermatitis enteropathica is caused by mutations in ZIP4 (SLC39A4), the intestinal zinc importer in the duodenum and jejunum. It presents with the classic triad: periorificial/acral dermatitis, alopecia, and diarrhea. Breast milk contains a ligand facilitating zinc absorption; symptoms emerge on weaning. Treatment: oral zinc sulfate.

questions.q: A 28-year-old man presents with pruritic papules and burrows in the finger web spaces, wrists, and genitalia. His partner has similar symptoms. KOH mount of burrow scrapings shows a mite with 8 legs and triangular spines on the dorsum. Correct management is:
opts: Treat index patient only with topical ivermectin 1% lotion
Permethrin 5% cream overnight for all household contacts simultaneously
Oral ivermectin 200 mcg/kg single dose for index patient only
Benzyl benzoate 25% applied for 3 consecutive days without treating contacts
questions.exp: Scabies caused by Sarcoptes scabiei is treated with permethrin 5% cream applied from neck to toes, left for 8-12 hours, and repeated after 1 week. Critically, all household and close contacts must be treated simultaneously to prevent re-infestation. Oral ivermectin 200 mcg/kg x2 doses (day 1 and 14) is an alternative, preferred for crusted scabies.

questions.q: A 45-year-old immunocompromised patient develops painful hemorrhagic bullae and eschar formation on the thigh after a minor injury. Wound culture grows gram-negative rods producing blue-green pigment on culture with a characteristic grape-like odor. The causative organism is:
questions.exp: Pseudomonas aeruginosa causes ecthyma gangrenosum: hemorrhagic bullae progressing to necrotic black eschars in immunocompromised patients, due to perivascular bacterial invasion and ischemic necrosis. It produces pyocyanin (blue-green), pyoverdin, and has a fruity/grape-like odor from 2-aminoacetophenone. Treatment: anti-pseudomonal beta-lactams.

questions.q: A 30-year-old woman with dermatomyositis has heliotrope rash, Gottron's papules, proximal muscle weakness, and anti-Jo-1 antibody. CPK is 2800 U/L. The antibody anti-Jo-1 is associated with which clinical syndrome?
opts: Antisynthetase syndrome with ILD, arthritis, and mechanic's hands
questions.exp: Anti-Jo-1 (anti-histidyl tRNA synthetase) is the most common antisynthetase antibody and defines the antisynthetase syndrome: inflammatory myopathy + interstitial lung disease + non-erosive arthritis + mechanic's hands + Raynaud's phenomenon + fever. ILD is the major cause of morbidity/mortality in these patients.

questions.q: A 20-year-old student presents with smooth, well-demarcated patches of hair loss on the scalp with no follicular remnants. Exclamation-mark hairs are seen at the patch margins. The underlying mechanism is:
opts: CD8+ T-cell attack on anagen hair bulb melanocytes (collapse of immune privilege)
questions.exp: Alopecia areata is a non-scarring alopecia caused by autoreactive CD8+ T cells attacking melanocyte-associated antigens in the anagen hair bulb, collapsing the hair follicle's immune privilege. Exclamation-mark hairs (proximal tapering, distal normal) are pathognomonic. JAK inhibitors (baricitinib, ritlecitinib) are FDA-approved for severe alopecia areata.

questions.q: A 55-year-old farmer from Maharashtra presents with indurated verrucous plaques on the dorsum of the foot and lower leg with black dot-like structures on the surface. Histopathology shows brown, thick-walled cells dividing by cross-septation (muriform cells). The diagnosis is:
questions.exp: Chromoblastomycosis is a chronic fungal infection caused by dematiaceous fungi (Fonsecaea pedrosoi is most common in India). The pathognomonic finding is Medlar bodies (sclerotic cells/muriform cells): brown, thick-walled cells with horizontal and vertical septation seen on histopathology. Treatment: itraconazole 200-400 mg/day + terbinafine.

questions.q: A 35-year-old woman presents with photosensitivity, malar rash, and positive lupus band test (LBT) on DIF of uninvolved sun-exposed skin. Which immunofluorescence pattern at the DEJ is MOST specific for systemic lupus erythematosus?
opts: Multiple immunoglobulins (IgG + IgM + IgA + C3) at DEJ
questions.exp: The lupus band test detects immune deposits at the DEJ on DIF. Multiple immunoglobulins (IgG + IgM + IgA) plus complement at the DEJ of uninvolved sun-exposed skin is most specific for SLE (~80% sensitivity). In discoid lupus erythematosus, only involved skin is positive. In SCLE, the LBT of uninvolved skin is usually negative.

questions.q: A patient presents with a solitary, painless, firm, skin-colored nodule on the lower leg that dimples inward on lateral compression (Fitzpatrick sign). Histopathology shows a storiform pattern of spindle cells with hemosiderin deposits. The diagnosis is:
questions.exp: Dermatofibroma (fibrous histiocytoma) produces Fitzpatrick sign: the lesion dimples inward when laterally compressed (opposite to lipoma/epidermoid cyst which protrude). Histology shows storiform-arranged fibroblasts with hemosiderin-laden macrophages and overlying epidermal hyperplasia. DFSP is CD34+, larger, and infiltrates fat in a lace-like pattern.

questions.q: A 42-year-old woman on dapsone for dermatitis herpetiformis develops sudden cyanosis unresponsive to oxygen, with chocolate-brown blood on venipuncture. ABG shows normal pO2 but SpO2 70% on pulse oximetry. The most appropriate antidote is:
questions.exp: Dapsone causes dose-dependent methemoglobinemia by oxidizing Hb Fe2+ to Fe3+, which cannot carry O2. Classic signs: cyanosis, chocolate-brown blood, normal pO2 but low SpO2 (pulse oximetry reads ~85% regardless of actual MetHb level). Methylene blue (1-2 mg/kg IV) reduces MetHb via NADPH-methemoglobin reductase. In G6PD deficiency, use ascorbic acid instead.

questions.q: A 25-year-old presents with grouped vesicles on an erythematous base on the elbows. Biopsy shows subepidermal blister with neutrophilic microabscesses in dermal papillae. DIF shows granular IgA deposits at the papillary tips. The most appropriate treatment is:
questions.exp: Dermatitis herpetiformis is associated with celiac disease (gluten-sensitive enteropathy). DIF showing granular IgA in dermal papillary tips is pathognomonic. Dapsone provides rapid symptomatic relief (within 24-48 hours) while the strict gluten-free diet slowly reverses intestinal changes, reduces IgA deposits, and decreases enteropathy-associated T-cell lymphoma risk.

questions.q: A 50-year-old man develops multiple flaccid bullae and erosions first on the oral mucosa then on the skin. Nikolsky sign is positive. DIF shows IgG and C3 in an intercellular 'chicken-wire' pattern throughout the epidermis. The target antigen is:
questions.exp: Pemphigus vulgaris targets desmoglein 3 (predominantly mucosal, causing oral lesions) and/or desmoglein 1 (superficial epidermis). Loss of desmoglein function causes acantholysis (loss of keratinocyte adhesion). Intercellular IgG on DIF (chicken-wire pattern) and positive Nikolsky sign are characteristic. First-line treatment is systemic corticosteroids with rituximab as steroid-sparing agent.

questions.q: A 68-year-old man with chronic sun damage presents with a 1.5 cm, rapidly growing nodule on the lower lip with central keratin-filled crater over 6 weeks. Biopsy shows well-differentiated squamous cells invading the dermis with perineural invasion. This feature is most concerning because:
opts: It indicates a keratoacanthoma-like growth pattern
Perineural invasion predicts high risk of metastasis and local spread
Lip location only confers moderate-risk status
questions.exp: SCC with perineural invasion is classified as high-risk with significantly elevated metastatic potential and risk of local recurrence. High-risk SCC features: diameter >2 cm, depth >4 mm, poor differentiation, perineural/vascular invasion, immunosuppression, ear/lip location. Mohs surgery is preferred; adjuvant radiotherapy may be required. Keratoacanthoma involutes spontaneously.

questions.q: A 30-year-old woman presents with mottled hyperpigmentation over the cheeks and upper lip symmetrically, worsening in summer and during her last pregnancy. Wood's lamp examination accentuates the hyperpigmentation. The most appropriate first-line treatment is:
opts: Oral tranexamic acid 500 mg twice daily alone
questions.exp: Melasma with epidermal predominance (Wood's lamp enhancement) responds best to triple combination cream (modified Kligman's formula): hydroquinone (tyrosinase inhibitor), tretinoin (increases epidermal turnover, facilitates HQ penetration), and mild corticosteroid (reduces irritation). Strict broad-spectrum photoprotection SPF 50+ is essential. Oral tranexamic acid is second-line adjunct.

questions.q: During a patch test for suspected allergic contact dermatitis, test substances are applied for 48 hours then read at 96 hours. A reaction showing erythema, infiltration, discrete vesicles, and bullae that spreads beyond the test site is graded as:
opts: ++ (strong positive: erythema, infiltration, papules, discrete vesicles)
+++ (extreme positive: coalescing vesicles, bullae, spreading beyond patch)
Irritant reaction (sharp demarcation, glazed surface, no spread)
questions.exp: ICDRG patch test grading: Negative (-): no reaction; Doubtful (?+): faint macular erythema; Weak positive (+): erythema, infiltration; Strong positive (++): erythema, infiltration, papules, discrete vesicles; Extreme positive (+++): bullous reaction spreading beyond patch area. Irritant reactions are sharply demarcated without spread and often show glazing/pustules.

questions.q: A 20-year-old student presents with pruritic, target-like lesions with three concentric zones on the palms and dorsa of hands following a fever and cold sores 10 days ago. Mucosal involvement is absent. The most likely precipitant is:
questions.exp: Erythema multiforme minor presents with classic target lesions (3 concentric zones) on acral sites without significant mucosal involvement. HSV reactivation (HSV-1 or 2) accounts for >70% of recurrent EM. The pathomechanism involves HSV DNA fragments triggering a cell-mediated immune response in the skin. Acyclovir prophylaxis prevents recurrences. Mycoplasma causes EM major/MIRM with mucosal predominance.
